t: The revolution began as a revolt against the abuses of Jo Byeong-gap, the magistrate of Gobu, and grew into a rising across Korea whose leaders were Donghak believers and whose armies were largely peasants.

After the Treaty of Jeonju of May 1894, the rebels ran much of south-west Korea through local offices called Jibgangso, until the arrival of Qing and Japanese troops and then the Japanese victory at Ugeumchi ended their hopes.

The rebel leaders were hanged in March 1895 and thousands of rebels were killed; some of their demands, such as the remarriage of widows and the freeing of enslaved people, were taken up in the Gabo Reform.
dyk: The rebels of 1894 followed rules that included not killing the innocent and paying for food in money rather than taking it, and they wore mostly white and carried bamboo spears, which gave rise to the saying "When sitting, a white mountain; when standing, a bamboo mountain."
ev: Southern Donghak believers petition for the religion's recognition and for the restoration of the honour of its founder
Rebels led by Jeon Bong-jun rise at Gobu against Jo Byeong-gap and defeat government forces at Hwangtojae and the Hwangryong River
The Treaty of Jeonju ends the first revolt, and the rebels govern much of the south-west
Qing and Japanese troops land at Incheon, and the First Sino-Japanese War begins
The rebel army is defeated at the Battle of Ugeumchi, and Jeon disbands it after Taein
At Jonggok on 18 December Japanese forces kill about 2,500 of 2,600 rebels, according to Japanese sources
Jeon Bong-jun and three other leaders are hanged for treason on 29 March

f.where: Korea, above all Jeolla Province, with fighting also in Chungcheong, Gyeongsang, Gyeonggi, Gangwon and Hwanghae.
f.period: The Gyojo Shinwon petitions (1892–1893); the Gobu revolt (January 1894); the first revolt and the Treaty of Jeonju (spring 1894); rebel rule in the south (summer 1894); the second revolt and the defeat at Ugeumchi (October–November 1894); executions and mopping-up (December 1894–1895).
f.figures: Jeon Bong-jun, leader of the revolt; Kim Gae-nam and Son Hwa-jung, his generals; Choe Sihyeong, the second leader of Donghak, who opposed the rebellion; Son Byong-hi, general of the Northern Jeob; Yi Bangeon, a Jeolla rebel leader; Kim Gu, the 'Baby Jeobju'.
f.outcome: The rebel armies were defeated, mainly by Japanese and government forces, and their leaders were captured and executed. Some of their demands later appeared in the Gabo Reform, and many survivors joined the Righteous Armies or the independence movement.
